statements.quote: This still was painted from a text prompt by a diffusion model.
The same family of machines now *animates* stills like this into coherent video — and a closely related family writes whole songs from a single line of text.
That is the story of this chapter.
\cite[Image: Stable Diffusion 3.5]{diffusion_astronaut_img}
In 1787 Mozart wrote down a card game.
Roll some dice, look up a table, and a little minuet you have never heard assembles itself bar by bar.
It was not artificial intelligence — it was a recipe for swapping interchangeable phrases.
But it already contained the whole idea: **music is recombination**, and if you can list the moves and the legal orderings, a machine can *choose* among them.

More than two centuries later, someone types a sentence into a box and a machine called **Sora** dreams up a full minute of video — a coherent little world with moving objects, a shifting camera, and, it turned out, a surprising sense of how physical things behave \cite[Sora (OpenAI, 2024)]{brooks2024sora}.

These are the same question asked twice: **can a machine make something that feels made?** And the punchline — the thing this chapter is really about — is that the machine that writes a three-minute song and the machine that renders a one-minute movie are, under the hood, *almost the same animal*.
They differ in one learned detail and share everything else.
Before there were deep neural networks, "a machine makes music" meant something else entirely.

statements.section: Music as information: the vocabulary

statements.quote: To generate music it first has to know what the *pieces* of music are, and how to represent them as numbers.
statements.section: Music as information: the vocabulary

statements.quote: So let's name the pieces — the minimal theory a model must capture — and then the two completely different ways music gets turned into data.
statements.section: Music as information: the vocabulary

statements.quote: A model does not learn a list of songs; it learns a *shape*.
statements.section: What a model has to capture

statements.quote: The space it moves through is not a filing cabinet of recordings but a curved, multi-scale landscape in which meaning is a property of *position*, not of any single point.
statements.section: What a model has to capture

statements.quote: A note is not located by one number but by a small stack of them: its **form** (what it is on its own), its **relation** (what it does to the notes around it), and its **situation** (what the whole passage is about).
statements.section: What a model has to capture

statements.quote: The model's job is not to find points but to follow the thin threads that run between them, stitching local, discrete events into one coherent whole \cite[Overview: music theory]{music_theory}.
statements.section: What a model has to capture

statements.quote: The pieces it must capture — the coordinates of that space — are:
statements.section: What a model has to capture

statements.quote: - **Pitch** is how high or low a note sounds; its physical cause is **frequency** in hertz.
statements.section: What a model has to capture

statements.quote: The reference note A above middle C — "concert pitch" — is standardized at **440 Hz**.
statements.section: What a model has to capture

statements.quote: - An **octave** is the interval where one frequency is exactly **double** the other; a note and the note an octave up have the same name.
statements.section: What a model has to capture

statements.quote: - Western keyboards divide the octave into **12 equal semitones** (*12-tone equal temperament*).
statements.section: What a model has to capture

statements.quote: Each semitone multiplies the frequency by $2^{1/12} \approx 1.0595$.
statements.section: What a model has to capture

statements.quote: This is why the piano keyboard is 12 keys to the octave.
statements.section: What a model has to capture

statements.quote: - A **scale** is a chosen set of notes; the **major scale** follows the whole/half-step pattern *whole–whole–half–whole–whole–whole–half*.
statements.section: What a model has to capture

statements.quote: **Major vs minor** differs mostly in the third (and sixth/seventh) degree: major sounds "bright," minor "darker." That one interval is most of why a minor key feels sad.
statements.section: What a model has to capture

statements.quote: - An **interval** is the distance between two pitches (counted in semitones, or as a frequency ratio).
statements.section: What a model has to capture

statements.quote: A **chord** is three or more notes sounded together; the basic one, a **triad**, is a root plus a third and a fifth.
statements.section: What a model has to capture

statements.quote: - **Rhythm** is the pattern of events in time; the **beat** is the steady pulse; **meter** is how beats are grouped (a *time signature* like 4/4).
statements.section: What a model has to capture

statements.quote: - **Timbre** ("tone colour") is what makes a piano and a violin playing the *same* note sound different.
statements.section: What a model has to capture

statements.quote: It is set not by the fundamental pitch but by the **harmonics** — the higher overtones riding on top — and by the note's loudness envelope (how it attacks and fades).
statements.section: What a model has to capture

statements.quote: - **Dynamics** is loudness: from *pp* (very soft) to *ff* (very loud).
statements.section: What a model has to capture

statements.quote: - **Form** is large-scale structure — verse, chorus, bridge, the ABAB or AABA shapes a song is built from.
statements.section: What a model has to capture

statements.quote: A music-generation model is learning the *joint statistics* of all of these at once: which chords follow which, how a melody leans over a harmony, how a snare sits in the meter, what "a warm cello" sounds like.
statements.section: What a model has to capture

statements.quote: There are **two fundamentally different representations** of music, and they led to two different machines.

statements.quote: For a long time, "music as data" meant **MIDI** — the *Musical Instrument Digital Interface*, a standard locked in in **1983** by Ikutaro Kakehashi of Roland, Dave Smith and Chet Wood of Sequential Circuits, and the other major synth makers (Yamaha, Korg, Kawai, Oberheim) \cite[How MIDI works]{midi}.
statements.section: The symbolic score: MIDI

statements.quote: MIDI does not store sound.
statements.section: The symbolic score: MIDI

statements.quote: It stores **instructions**: *note-on at pitch 60, velocity 80, now; note-off, 300 ms later; on channel 3*.
statements.section: The symbolic score: MIDI

statements.quote: It works across 16 channels, and it says nothing about timbre at all — the sound comes from whatever keyboard or software plays the file back.
statements.section: The symbolic score: MIDI

statements.quote: That is the whole point, and the whole limitation.
statements.section: The symbolic score: MIDI

statements.quote: MIDI is tiny and perfectly editable — you can quantize a note, transpose a chord, re-velocity a phrase — but it is a **score, not a recording**.
statements.section: The symbolic score: MIDI

statements.quote: It cannot carry the sound of a specific singer, the room of a specific studio, the grit of a specific guitar.
statements.section: The symbolic score: MIDI

statements.quote: A model that only sees MIDI can write *notes*; it cannot write *sound*.
statements.section: The symbolic score: MIDI

statements.quote: It sends *note* messages — not sound — to a computer or synth, which is exactly what makes MIDI "music as data": a symbolic score you can edit, quantize and transpose, but which carries no actual audio.

statements.quote: This is **PCM** (pulse-code modulation): you measure the pressure of the air many thousands of times a second and store each measurement as a number \cite[How sound is digitized: PCM]{pcm}.
statements.section: The raw wave: PCM

statements.quote: Two numbers govern it all, and the second is a theorem.
statements.section: The raw wave: PCM

statements.quote: The **Nyquist–Shannon sampling theorem** says a signal can be perfectly reconstructed only if you sample it **faster than twice its highest frequency** \cite[Nyquist–Shannon sampling theorem]{nyquist_sampling}.

statements.section: So what was the "first" audio format?

statements.quote: - The first widely-adopted **digital** audio format was the **CD** (1982) — DAT (1987) was the other early digital medium, but it stayed in studios.
statements.section: So what was the "first" audio format?

statements.quote: - The first popular **lossy-compressed** format was the **MP3** (standardized 1993).
statements.section: So what was the "first" audio format?

statements.quote: The CD solved *storing* sound, but 2.6 million numbers a minute was too big to stream or fit on the small memory of the 1990s.
statements.section: Compression and the ear: how MP3 works

statements.quote: The **MP3** — MPEG-1 Audio **Layer III**, standardized in **1993** by the Fraunhofer Society under Karlheinz Brandenburg, merging Fraunhofer's ASPEC with the French CCETT group's MUSICAM \cite[How MP3 works]{mp3} — solved *shrinking* it, and it did so with a genuinely clever idea: **the ear is not a perfect recorder, so throw away what it cannot hear.**
statements.section: Compression and the ear: how MP3 works

statements.quote: The ear has blind spots, and MP3 exploits two of them:
statements.section: Hiding the loss: psychoacoustics

statements.quote: - **Simultaneous (spectral) masking**: a loud tone makes quieter tones *at nearby frequencies* inaudible.
statements.section: Hiding the loss: psychoacoustics

statements.quote: Play a loud A and a soft B next to it and you stop hearing the B.
statements.section: Hiding the loss: psychoacoustics

statements.quote: - **Temporal masking**: a sudden loud sound blinds the ear for a few milliseconds *before* it (pre-masking) and tens of milliseconds *after* (post-masking).
statements.section: Hiding the loss: psychoacoustics

statements.quote: A psychoacoustic model computes a **masking threshold** at every moment and every frequency — the floor below which sound is inaudible.
statements.section: Hiding the loss: psychoacoustics

statements.quote: MP3 then simply does not spend bits there.
statements.section: Hiding the loss: psychoacoustics

statements.quote: That is the entire loss: it is *perceptual*, not mathematical.
statements.section: Hiding the loss: psychoacoustics

statements.quote: To act on frequencies, MP3 must move from the time domain (the waveform) to the frequency domain.
statements.section: Turning time into frequencies: the MDCT

statements.quote: It does this with the **modified discrete cosine transform (MDCT)**, a cousin of the DCT that chops the signal into short overlapping windows (50% overlap) so the transform has good resolution in both time and frequency \cite[The MDCT]{mdct}.
statements.section: Turning time into frequencies: the MDCT

statements.quote: In each window it **allocates bits by sensitivity**: full precision where the ear is sharp, almost nothing where a masking threshold hides it.
statements.section: Turning time into frequencies: the MDCT

statements.quote: A spectrogram — time across, frequency up, brightness for loudness.
statements.section: Turning time into frequencies: the MDCT

statements.quote: This is the view a perceptual coder actually works on: MP3's MDCT turns the waveform into a picture like this and then deletes the parts the ear would not miss.
statements.section: Turning time into frequencies: the MDCT

statements.quote: A modern neural codec does the same job, but *learns* what to keep.
statements.section: Turning time into frequencies: the MDCT

statements.quote: \cite[Image: Sagenat2, CC BY-SA 4.0]{audio_spectrogram_img}
statements.section: Turning time into frequencies: the MDCT

statements.quote: The three **layers** of MPEG-1 audio are just three levels of this trade-off (Layer I simplest, Layer II sub-band, **Layer III = MP3** most efficient).
statements.section: Turning time into frequencies: the MDCT

statements.quote: The result was a ~10× shrink that *sounded* like the CD — and it became the format of the internet age.
statements.section: Turning time into frequencies: the MDCT

statements.quote: MP3's core insight — *discard the inaudible, learned or otherwise* — is exactly what a **neural audio codec** does, but end-to-end and with no hand-designed psychoacoustic model.
statements.section: The heir to MP3: the neural audio codec

statements.quote: **SoundStream** (Google, 2021) (\cite[Zeghidour et al., 2021]{zeghidour2021soundstream}) and **EnCodec** (Meta, 2022) (\cite[Defossez et al., 2022]{defossez2022encodec}) learn a compression that matches what MP3 achieves at a fraction of the bitrate.

statements.quote: And they do it in a way that sets up the deep-learning story perfectly: **they turn the waveform into a short list of discrete codes.** That is the bridge from a song to a sequence a Transformer can read.

statements.quote: Before we generate anything, we have to name the machine doing the generating.
statements.section: The engine: transformers and attention

statements.quote: Both the song-writer and the video-writer are built on the same engine: the **transformer**, whose defining idea is **self-attention** (\cite[Vaswani et al., 2017]{vaswani2017attention}).
statements.section: The engine: transformers and attention

statements.quote: (The full architecture is the subject of the **Attention** chapter; here is how it is used to *generate*.)
statements.section: The engine: transformers and attention

statements.quote: Strip a modern model to one repeating block and it does four things, in order:
statements.section: What a transformer block actually does

statements.quote: **Self-attention** — let every position look at every other position and decide what to blend in.
statements.section: What a transformer block actually does

statements.quote: A **feed-forward network** (two matrix multiplies with a non-linearity) applied to each position on its own.
statements.section: What a transformer block actually does

statements.quote: A **residual connection** around each of the two — the input is added back, so gradients flow and deep networks train.
statements.section: What a transformer block actually does

statements.quote: A **layer norm** to keep the activations at a stable scale.
statements.section: What a transformer block actually does

statements.quote: At the very start, each token is turned into a vector (its **embedding**) plus a **position** signal; at the very end, a linear layer turns the final vectors into a probability over the vocabulary.
statements.section: What a transformer block actually does

statements.quote: Stack a few dozen of these blocks and you have GPT, MusicGen, and the denoiser inside Sora.
statements.section: What a transformer block actually does

statements.quote: Read it as: *compare my query to everyone's key, turn the matches into weights, and return a weighted blend of everyone's values.* It is **content-based routing** — unlike a convolution, which only looks at fixed neighbours, or a recurrence, which only looks left-to-right, attention can link token 1 directly to token 5000 in a single step.
statements.section: Attention: learned "who looks at whom"

statements.quote: Split the computation across several **heads** (multi-head attention) and the model can track many kinds of relationships at once — melody against harmony, this object against that surface.
statements.section: Attention: learned "who looks at whom"

statements.quote: Self-attention lets the model talk to itself.
statements.section: Cross-attention: how the prompt steers the machine

statements.quote: **Cross-attention** lets it talk to *you*.
statements.section: Cross-attention: how the prompt steers the machine

statements.quote: The query still comes from the tokens being generated, but the keys and values come from a **different** sequence — your text prompt, first run through a transformer **encoder** like CLIP (\cite[Radford et al., 2021]{radford2021clip}) or T5.
statements.section: Cross-attention: how the prompt steers the machine

statements.quote: At every step the model asks the words in your prompt "which part of this should you be steering?" The word *"cello"* claims the low, warm frequencies; *"fast"* claims the tempo.
statements.section: Cross-attention: how the prompt steers the machine

statements.quote: This is the same mechanism that makes a text-to-*image* model paint what you ask for — the reason your prompt has any effect at all.
statements.section: Cross-attention: how the prompt steers the machine

statements.quote: A raw sequence has no built-in sense of order, so the model is given **positional encodings** — a signal telling each token where it sits in the sequence (a learned vector, or a smooth function of its index).
statements.section: Position: how the model knows "next"

statements.quote: For music and video this is essential: *order is the whole point*.
statements.section: Position: how the model knows "next"

statements.quote: A melody is a specific order of notes; a video is a specific order of frames.
statements.section: Position: how the model knows "next"

statements.quote: In Sora the position signal is **three-dimensional**, because a token's "where" has width, height, *and* time.
statements.section: Position: how the model knows "next"

statements.quote: You could have built these machines on older ideas — recurrent networks like WaveNet (\cite[van den Oord et al., 2016]{oord2016wavenet}) did, at first.
statements.section: Why transformers won

statements.quote: They mostly lost for the reason Rich Sutton called **the Bitter Lesson** (\cite[Sutton, 2019]{sutton2019bitter}): methods that scale with compute and data beat cleverly hand-crafted ones.
statements.section: Why transformers won

statements.quote: The transformer's **next-token** objective is *modality-agnostic* — it does not care whether the tokens are words, audio codes, or video patches — and attention gives it long-range reach at fixed depth.
statements.section: Why transformers won

statements.quote: Same architecture, new vocabulary, more data.
statements.section: Why transformers won

statements.quote: That is the whole recipe, and it is why one codebase keeps becoming the next breakthrough.

statements.quote: Given a tokenizer that turns a signal into tokens, and a transformer engine, there are **two** fundamentally different ways to turn "a prompt" into "a song" or "a clip." They are both transformers at the core; they differ in *how the sequence is produced*.

statements.quote: Knowing both is the key to reading every paper in this field.
statements.section: The two ways to generate

statements.quote: This is the LLM way, applied to sound.

statements.quote: The model predicts the **next token** given everything so far — exactly as GPT predicts the next word — and it just keeps going.

statements.quote: A whole song is too long to predict flatly, so the serious autoregressive machines build it **coarse-to-fine**, in layers of tokens at different rates:
statements.section: Building a song in layers

statements.quote: - **AudioLM** (Google, 2023) first autoregressively writes low-rate **semantic tokens** that carry long-range structure — *this is the verse, the harmony drifts here* — and then a second, non-autoregressive stage fills in the high-rate **acoustic tokens** (the actual codec codes) that a decoder turns back into sound (\cite[Borsos et al., 2023]{borsos2023audiolm}).
statements.section: Building a song in layers

statements.quote: - **MusicLM** (Google, 2023) does the same as a hierarchy: a **slow** transformer lays down melody, harmony and rhythm over long timescales, a **fast** transformer adds timbre and detail, and a vocoder renders audio — which is what lets it stay coherent for *minutes* (\cite[Agostinelli et al., 2023]{agostinelli2023musiqlm}).
statements.section: Building a song in layers

statements.quote: - **MusicGen** (Meta, 2023) is the lean, open, fast version: a single transformer over EnCodec's stacked codebooks, writing them token by token, steered by a text embedding (\cite[Copet et al., 2023]{copet2023musicgen}).

statements.quote: MusicLM generates high-fidelity music from text descriptions such as "a calming violin melody backed by a distorted guitar riff", remaining consistent over several minutes.

statements.quote: First a **variational autoencoder** (a VAE, \cite[Kingma & Welling, 2013]{kingma2014vae}) compresses the signal into a small **latent** space that keeps the important content and throws away the predictable detail.
statements.section: The latent space and the denoiser

statements.quote: This is the same "space of coherent relations" from the vocabulary section, seen from the other end: the codec has folded the raw signal into the small set of coordinates the model actually reasons over.
statements.section: The latent space and the denoiser

statements.quote: The diffusion process then runs in this compact space: a network is trained to predict *the noise that was added* at each of many steps, and at generation time you start from random latent noise and denoise it step by step until a clean, novel clip or track appears (\cite[Rombach et al., 2022]{rombach2022ldm}).

statements.quote: The original diffusion denoisers were **U-Nets** — convolutional image networks.
statements.section: The Diffusion Transformer: the unlock for video

statements.quote: In 2023, Peebles and Xie showed you can replace the U-Net with a **transformer that operates on patches** of the latent — a **Diffusion Transformer, or DiT** (\cite[Peebles & Xie, 2023]{peebles2023dit}).

statements.quote: Two changes make it a big deal:
statements.section: The Diffusion Transformer: the unlock for video

statements.quote: - The latent is cut into a grid of **patches**, each patch becoming a **token**, and the transformer attends over all of them — so the denoiser is now structurally *the same family* as an LLM.

statements.quote: - The timestep and the prompt are injected by **modulating the layer norms** (a trick called **adaLN**) rather than stitched in by hand, so the model always knows *how noisy* the input is and *what it was asked for*.

statements.quote: This was the architectural unlock for video: once the denoiser was a transformer over patches, you could scale it with everything else — and that is exactly what Sora did.

statements.quote: Zoom out and the story is one long arc with two turns.
statements.section: The question, answered — differently

statements.quote: The first was philosophical: *remove the composer's hand* — Mozart's dice, Cage's stalks, Mälzel's self-playing organ, Xenakis' probabilities.
statements.section: The question, answered — differently

statements.quote: The second is the one this chapter is about: *stop writing the rules, and let a big model infer them from the world* — until the machine can, from a sentence, dream a song or a world.
statements.section: The question, answered — differently

statements.quote: Music generation and video generation look like two different miracles to a first-time user.
statements.section: The question, answered — differently

statements.quote: They are the same miracle seen from two angles: **a signal, compressed into tokens, then written by a transformer.** The dice are still there — a diffusion model "rolls the dice" in latent space at every denoising step, and a language model rolls them at every sampling step — but now the dice are guided by a prompt, and the table they roll on is a statistical model of reality.
statements.section: The question, answered — differently

statements.quote: More than two centuries after Mozart rolled the dice, the question "can a machine make something that feels made?" has a working, if contested, *yes*.
statements.section: The question, answered — differently

statements.quote: The open questions are the human ones — who made it, who owns it, and what we do with a machine that can dream in audio and video.

blocks.quote: This still was painted from a text prompt by a diffusion model. The same family of machines now *animates* stills like this into coherent video — and a closely related family writes whole songs from a single line of text. That is the story of this chapter. \cite[Image: Stable Diffusion 3.5]{diffusion_astronaut_img}

In 1787 Mozart wrote down a card game. Roll some dice, look up a table, and a little minuet you have never heard assembles itself bar by bar. It was not artificial intelligence — it was a recipe for swapping interchangeable phrases. But it already contained the whole idea: **music is recombination**, and if you can list the moves and the legal orderings, a machine can *choose* among them.

More than two centuries later, someone types a sentence into a box and a machine called **Sora** dreams up a full minute of video — a coherent little world with moving objects, a shifting camera, and, it turned out, a surprising sense of how physical things behave \cite[Sora (OpenAI, 2024)]{brooks2024sora}.

These are the same question asked twice: **can a machine make something that feels made?** And the punchline — the thing this chapter is really about — is that the machine that writes a three-minute song and the machine that renders a one-minute movie are, under the hood, *almost the same animal*. They differ in one learned detail and share everything else.
The long road to a machine that composes
blocks.section: The long road to a machine that composes

blocks.quote: Before there were deep neural networks, "a machine makes music" meant something else entirely. For most of that time it meant *a machine follows a recipe a human wrote, with a little randomness stirred in*. Understanding that older meaning makes the deep-learning era land harder.
blocks.section: The long road to a machine that composes

blocks.quote: Machines that make music without ears
blocks.section: Machines that make music without ears

blocks.quote: The oldest trick is to **remove the composer's hand**. In the 1910s Marcel Duchamp let chance pick the notes of a "score" that was really a joke about the pretensions of music. In 1951 John Cage composed *Music of Changes* by consulting the *I Ching*, throwing stalks to decide pitch and duration — deliberately emptying intention out of the piece. The question was never "can we make good music?" It was "what is left of *composition* when the decisions come from somewhere else?"
blocks.section: Machines that make music without ears

blocks.quote: The machines were already hinting at the answer, mechanically. In **1805** the instrument-maker Johann Nepomuk Mälzel built the **Panharmonicon** (\cite[Mälzel's Panharmonicon, 1805]{panharmonicon}), a large organ-like machine that could *play itself* — an automatic player that imitated a whole orchestra and even cannon fire. Beethoven later wrote *Wellington's Victory* (1813) for it. It was not a composer; it was a very elaborate pinball of sound. But a walking, self-playing orchestra was the first time a *device*, not a person, performed a complete piece — the ancestor of every "generative" music system since.
blocks.section: Machines that make music without ears

blocks.quote: When computers put their hands on the piano
blocks.section: When computers put their hands on the piano

blocks.quote: When the first real computers appeared, the question became engineering. In **1951** a machine called **CSIRAC**, then in Sydney, played *Colonel Bogey* — among the earliest computer music. That same year Christopher Strachey ran a program on a Ferranti Mark 1 in Manchester that produced another early example of computer music (\cite[Strachey, 1951]{strachey1952}). In **1957** a composer, Leonard Isaacson, and a mathematician, Lejaren Hiller, wrote the **Illiac Suite** for string quartet on the ILLIAC I — the first major work a computer *composed* \cite[Hiller & Isaacson's Illiac Suite]{illiac_suite}. And that same year, **Max Mathews** wrote **MUSIC**, the first computer language for *synthesizing* sound in real time \cite[Max Mathews and MUSIC]{max_mathews} — the moment the computer stopped being a calculator and became an **instrument**.
blocks.section: When computers put their hands on the piano

blocks.quote: Around the same years the composer **Iannis Xenakis** went further: in *Pithoprakta* (1955) and, in 1962, *ST/10* and *Atrées* realised on an IBM 7090, he placed notes with **probability distributions** rather than rules a person could follow. Math, not taste, was the composer.
blocks.section: When computers put their hands on the piano

blocks.quote: > The seed of everything in this chapter is a question the art world raised in 1951: if a machine, or a die, makes the choices, is it still composition — and who is the composer?
blocks.section: When computers put their hands on the piano

blocks.quote: Music as information: the vocabulary
blocks.section: Music as information: the vocabulary

blocks.quote: A machine cannot "hear" the way you do. To generate music it first has to know what the *pieces* of music are, and how to represent them as numbers. So let's name the pieces — the minimal theory a model must capture — and then the two completely different ways music gets turned into data.
blocks.section: Music as information: the vocabulary

blocks.quote: What a model has to capture
blocks.section: What a model has to capture

blocks.quote: A model does not learn a list of songs; it learns a *shape*. The space it moves through is not a filing cabinet of recordings but a curved, multi-scale landscape in which meaning is a property of *position*, not of any single point. A note is not located by one number but by a small stack of them: its **form** (what it is on its own), its **relation** (what it does to the notes around it), and its **situation** (what the whole passage is about). The model's job is not to find points but to follow the thin threads that run between them, stitching local, discrete events into one coherent whole \cite[Overview: music theory]{music_theory}. The pieces it must capture — the coordinates of that space — are:
blocks.section: What a model has to capture

blocks.quote: - **Pitch** is how high or low a note sounds; its physical cause is **frequency** in hertz. The reference note A above middle C — "concert pitch" — is standardized at **440 Hz**.
blocks.section: What a model has to capture

blocks.quote: - An **octave** is the interval where one frequency is exactly **double** the other; a note and the note an octave up have the same name.
blocks.section: What a model has to capture

blocks.quote: - Western keyboards divide the octave into **12 equal semitones** (*12-tone equal temperament*). Each semitone multiplies the frequency by $2^{1/12} \approx 1.0595$. This is why the piano keyboard is 12 keys to the octave.
blocks.section: What a model has to capture

blocks.quote: - A **scale** is a chosen set of notes; the **major scale** follows the whole/half-step pattern *whole–whole–half–whole–whole–whole–half*. **Major vs minor** differs mostly in the third (and sixth/seventh) degree: major sounds "bright," minor "darker." That one interval is most of why a minor key feels sad.
blocks.section: What a model has to capture

blocks.quote: - An **interval** is the distance between two pitches (counted in semitones, or as a frequency ratio). A **chord** is three or more notes sounded together; the basic one, a **triad**, is a root plus a third and a fifth.
blocks.section: What a model has to capture

blocks.quote: - **Rhythm** is the pattern of events in time; the **beat** is the steady pulse; **meter** is how beats are grouped (a *time signature* like 4/4).
blocks.section: What a model has to capture

blocks.quote: - **Timbre** ("tone colour") is what makes a piano and a violin playing the *same* note sound different. It is set not by the fundamental pitch but by the **harmonics** — the higher overtones riding on top — and by the note's loudness envelope (how it attacks and fades).
blocks.section: What a model has to capture

blocks.quote: - **Dynamics** is loudness: from *pp* (very soft) to *ff* (very loud).
blocks.section: What a model has to capture

blocks.quote: - **Form** is large-scale structure — verse, chorus, bridge, the ABAB or AABA shapes a song is built from.
blocks.section: What a model has to capture

blocks.quote: A music-generation model is learning the *joint statistics* of all of these at once: which chords follow which, how a melody leans over a harmony, how a snare sits in the meter, what "a warm cello" sounds like.
blocks.section: What a model has to capture

blocks.quote: Two ways to write it down
blocks.section: Two ways to write it down

blocks.quote: Here is the crucial fork in the road, and it shapes everything after it. There are **two fundamentally different representations** of music, and they led to two different machines.
blocks.section: Two ways to write it down

blocks.quote: The symbolic score: MIDI
blocks.section: The symbolic score: MIDI

blocks.quote: For a long time, "music as data" meant **MIDI** — the *Musical Instrument Digital Interface*, a standard locked in in **1983** by Ikutaro Kakehashi of Roland, Dave Smith and Chet Wood of Sequential Circuits, and the other major synth makers (Yamaha, Korg, Kawai, Oberheim) \cite[How MIDI works]{midi}. MIDI does not store sound. It stores **instructions**: *note-on at pitch 60, velocity 80, now; note-off, 300 ms later; on channel 3*. It works across 16 channels, and it says nothing about timbre at all — the sound comes from whatever keyboard or software plays the file back.
blocks.section: The symbolic score: MIDI

blocks.quote: That is the whole point, and the whole limitation. MIDI is tiny and perfectly editable — you can quantize a note, transpose a chord, re-velocity a phrase — but it is a **score, not a recording**. It cannot carry the sound of a specific singer, the room of a specific studio, the grit of a specific guitar. A model that only sees MIDI can write *notes*; it cannot write *sound*.
blocks.section: The symbolic score: MIDI

blocks.quote: A MIDI controller. It sends *note* messages — not sound — to a computer or synth, which is exactly what makes MIDI "music as data": a symbolic score you can edit, quantize and transpose, but which carries no actual audio. \cite[Photo: Melissa Goldsmith, CC BY-SA 4.0]{midi_keyboard_img}
blocks.section: The symbolic score: MIDI

blocks.quote: The raw wave: PCM
blocks.section: The raw wave: PCM

blocks.quote: The other representation is the **recording** — the air-pressure wave itself, sampled into numbers. This is **PCM** (pulse-code modulation): you measure the pressure of the air many thousands of times a second and store each measurement as a number \cite[How sound is digitized: PCM]{pcm}.
blocks.section: The raw wave: PCM

blocks.quote: Two numbers govern it all, and the second is a theorem. The **Nyquist–Shannon sampling theorem** says a signal can be perfectly reconstructed only if you sample it **faster than twice its highest frequency** \cite[Nyquist–Shannon sampling theorem]{nyquist_sampling}. Human hearing tops out near 20 kHz, so you must sample above 40 kHz. The Compact Disc standard, the 1980 "Red Book," chose **44,100 samples per second**, each stored as a **16-bit** number (65,536 levels, about 96 dB of dynamic range) \cite[CD-DA and the Red Book]{cd_digital_audio}.
blocks.section: The raw wave: PCM

blocks.quote: A CD-quality minute of music is therefore about **2.6 million numbers**. That is the raw material — and it is far too dense for any model to chew directly.
blocks.section: The raw wave: PCM

blocks.quote: Sound made visible. An oscilloscope shows a tone as a wave over time — a sine wave is a pure single frequency, a square wave is the same note stacked with its odd harmonics. PCM digitizes exactly this: it stamps the height of the wave at 44,100 points per second. \cite[Photo: Xato, public domain]{oscilloscope_waveform_img}
blocks.section: The raw wave: PCM

blocks.quote: From wax to numbers: the audio format story
blocks.section: From wax to numbers: the audio format story

blocks.quote: Before a neural network ever compressed a song, a century of engineers did it by hand — first to *store* sound, then to *shrink* it. The story matters, because the modern neural audio codec is a direct heir of the oldest trick in this part: **throw away what the ear won't notice.**
blocks.section: From wax to numbers: the audio format story

blocks.quote: Analog: grooves, tape, and the voice in the box
blocks.section: Analog: grooves, tape, and the voice in the box

blocks.quote: The **phonograph** (Thomas Edison, 1877) cut a spiral groove into wax; a stylus reading the groove turned geometry back into sound. **Magnetic tape** (AEG's Magnetophon, 1935; the Ampex 200 in the US, 1948) recorded a magnetized strip instead — edit by splicing, copy by duplicating. The **vinyl LP** (Columbia, 1948) put a high-fidelity groove on a durable disc, and the **compact cassette** (Philips, 1963) put a tiny tape in your pocket. All of these are *analog*: the groove, the magnetization, the groove again — a continuous physical trace of the wave.
blocks.section: Analog: grooves, tape, and the voice in the box

blocks.quote: Long-playing record, 1948. The sound lives in the shape of the groove — a purely analog trace. Every copy is a physical re-recording of the wave, which is why records hiss and degrade in a way a digital file never does. \cite[Photo: Evan-Amos, public domain]{vinyl_lp_record_img}
blocks.section: Analog: grooves, tape, and the voice in the box

blocks.quote: Digital: the Red Book and the number 44,100
blocks.section: Digital: the Red Book and the number 44,100

blocks.quote: The digital era began when sound was converted to the PCM numbers above. **DAT** (Digital Audio Tape, Sony, 1987) digitized studio tape. But the format that changed everything was the **Compact Disc**: launched in **1982** by Sony and Philips, governed by the 1980 **Red Book** standard that fixed audio at **44.1 kHz / 16-bit** \cite[CD-DA and the Red Book]{cd_digital_audio}. A CD does not wear, does not hiss, and can be copied with perfect fidelity — because it stores *numbers*, not grooves.
blocks.section: Digital: the Red Book and the number 44,100

blocks.quote: The compact disc (1982). Its surface is a laser-readable spiral of 0s and 1s — the first mass-market place for the 44.1 kHz / 16-bit PCM standard. \cite[Photo: liamz2r, public domain]{cd_compact_disc_img}
blocks.section: Digital: the Red Book and the number 44,100

blocks.quote: So what was the "first" audio format?
blocks.section: So what was the "first" audio format?

blocks.quote: It is a trick question, because "first" depends on which category you mean:
blocks.section: So what was the "first" audio format?

blocks.quote: - The first widely-adopted **digital** audio format was the **CD** (1982) — DAT (1987) was the other early digital medium, but it stayed in studios.
blocks.section: So what was the "first" audio format?

blocks.quote: - The first popular **lossy-compressed** format was the **MP3** (standardized 1993).
blocks.section: So what was the "first" audio format?

blocks.quote: So: *digital* in 1982, *compressed* in 1993.
blocks.section: So what was the "first" audio format?

blocks.quote: Compression and the ear: how MP3 works
blocks.section: Compression and the ear: how MP3 works

blocks.quote: The CD solved *storing* sound, but 2.6 million numbers a minute was too big to stream or fit on the small memory of the 1990s. The **MP3** — MPEG-1 Audio **Layer III**, standardized in **1993** by the Fraunhofer Society under Karlheinz Brandenburg, merging Fraunhofer's ASPEC with the French CCETT group's MUSICAM \cite[How MP3 works]{mp3} — solved *shrinking* it, and it did so with a genuinely clever idea: **the ear is not a perfect recorder, so throw away what it cannot hear.**
blocks.section: Compression and the ear: how MP3 works

blocks.quote: Hiding the loss: psychoacoustics
blocks.section: Hiding the loss: psychoacoustics

blocks.quote: The ear has blind spots, and MP3 exploits two of them:
blocks.section: Hiding the loss: psychoacoustics

blocks.quote: - **Simultaneous (spectral) masking**: a loud tone makes quieter tones *at nearby frequencies* inaudible. Play a loud A and a soft B next to it and you stop hearing the B.
blocks.section: Hiding the loss: psychoacoustics

blocks.quote: - **Temporal masking**: a sudden loud sound blinds the ear for a few milliseconds *before* it (pre-masking) and tens of milliseconds *after* (post-masking).
blocks.section: Hiding the loss: psychoacoustics

blocks.quote: A psychoacoustic model computes a **masking threshold** at every moment and every frequency — the floor below which sound is inaudible. MP3 then simply does not spend bits there. That is the entire loss: it is *perceptual*, not mathematical.
blocks.section: Hiding the loss: psychoacoustics

blocks.quote: Turning time into frequencies: the MDCT
blocks.section: Turning time into frequencies: the MDCT

blocks.quote: To act on frequencies, MP3 must move from the time domain (the waveform) to the frequency domain. It does this with the **modified discrete cosine transform (MDCT)**, a cousin of the DCT that chops the signal into short overlapping windows (50% overlap) so the transform has good resolution in both time and frequency \cite[The MDCT]{mdct}. In each window it **allocates bits by sensitivity**: full precision where the ear is sharp, almost nothing where a masking threshold hides it.
blocks.section: Turning time into frequencies: the MDCT

blocks.quote: A spectrogram — time across, frequency up, brightness for loudness. This is the view a perceptual coder actually works on: MP3's MDCT turns the waveform into a picture like this and then deletes the parts the ear would not miss. A modern neural codec does the same job, but *learns* what to keep. \cite[Image: Sagenat2, CC BY-SA 4.0]{audio_spectrogram_img}
blocks.section: Turning time into frequencies: the MDCT

blocks.quote: The three **layers** of MPEG-1 audio are just three levels of this trade-off (Layer I simplest, Layer II sub-band, **Layer III = MP3** most efficient). The result was a ~10× shrink that *sounded* like the CD — and it became the format of the internet age.
blocks.section: Turning time into frequencies: the MDCT

blocks.quote: The heir to MP3: the neural audio codec
blocks.section: The heir to MP3: the neural audio codec

blocks.quote: MP3's core insight — *discard the inaudible, learned or otherwise* — is exactly what a **neural audio codec** does, but end-to-end and with no hand-designed psychoacoustic model. **SoundStream** (Google, 2021) (\cite[Zeghidour et al., 2021]{zeghidour2021soundstream}) and **EnCodec** (Meta, 2022) (\cite[Defossez et al., 2022]{defossez2022encodec}) learn a compression that matches what MP3 achieves at a fraction of the bitrate. And they do it in a way that sets up the deep-learning story perfectly: **they turn the waveform into a short list of discrete codes.** That is the bridge from a song to a sequence a Transformer can read. We will build that codec, brick by brick, in a moment.
blocks.section: The heir to MP3: the neural audio codec

blocks.quote: The engine: transformers and attention
blocks.section: The engine: transformers and attention

blocks.quote: Before we generate anything, we have to name the machine doing the generating. Both the song-writer and the video-writer are built on the same engine: the **transformer**, whose defining idea is **self-attention** (\cite[Vaswani et al., 2017]{vaswani2017attention}). (The full architecture is the subject of the **Attention** chapter; here is how it is used to *generate*.)
blocks.section: The engine: transformers and attention

blocks.quote: What a transformer block actually does
blocks.section: What a transformer block actually does

blocks.quote: Strip a modern model to one repeating block and it does four things, in order:
blocks.section: What a transformer block actually does

blocks.quote: 1. **Self-attention** — let every position look at every other position and decide what to blend in.
blocks.section: What a transformer block actually does

blocks.quote: 2. A **feed-forward network** (two matrix multiplies with a non-linearity) applied to each position on its own.
blocks.section: What a transformer block actually does

blocks.quote: 3. A **residual connection** around each of the two — the input is added back, so gradients flow and deep networks train.
blocks.section: What a transformer block actually does

blocks.quote: 4. A **layer norm** to keep the activations at a stable scale.
blocks.section: What a transformer block actually does

blocks.quote: At the very start, each token is turned into a vector (its **embedding**) plus a **position** signal; at the very end, a linear layer turns the final vectors into a probability over the vocabulary. Stack a few dozen of these blocks and you have GPT, MusicGen, and the denoiser inside Sora.
blocks.section: What a transformer block actually does

blocks.quote: Attention: learned "who looks at whom"
blocks.section: Attention: learned "who looks at whom"

blocks.quote: Read it as: *compare my query to everyone's key, turn the matches into weights, and return a weighted blend of everyone's values.* It is **content-based routing** — unlike a convolution, which only looks at fixed neighbours, or a recurrence, which only looks left-to-right, attention can link token 1 directly to token 5000 in a single step. Split the computation across several **heads** (multi-head attention) and the model can track many kinds of relationships at once — melody against harmony, this object against that surface.
blocks.section: Attention: learned "who looks at whom"

blocks.quote: Cross-attention: how the prompt steers the machine
blocks.section: Cross-attention: how the prompt steers the machine

blocks.quote: Self-attention lets the model talk to itself. **Cross-attention** lets it talk to *you*. The query still comes from the tokens being generated, but the keys and values come from a **different** sequence — your text prompt, first run through a transformer **encoder** like CLIP (\cite[Radford et al., 2021]{radford2021clip}) or T5. At every step the model asks the words in your prompt "which part of this should you be steering?" The word *"cello"* claims the low, warm frequencies; *"fast"* claims the tempo. This is the same mechanism that makes a text-to-*image* model paint what you ask for — the reason your prompt has any effect at all.
blocks.section: Cross-attention: how the prompt steers the machine

blocks.quote: Position: how the model knows "next"
blocks.section: Position: how the model knows "next"

blocks.quote: A raw sequence has no built-in sense of order, so the model is given **positional encodings** — a signal telling each token where it sits in the sequence (a learned vector, or a smooth function of its index). For music and video this is essential: *order is the whole point*. A melody is a specific order of notes; a video is a specific order of frames. In Sora the position signal is **three-dimensional**, because a token's "where" has width, height, *and* time.
blocks.section: Position: how the model knows "next"

blocks.quote: Why transformers won
blocks.section: Why transformers won

blocks.quote: You could have built these machines on older ideas — recurrent networks like WaveNet (\cite[van den Oord et al., 2016]{oord2016wavenet}) did, at first. They mostly lost for the reason Rich Sutton called **the Bitter Lesson** (\cite[Sutton, 2019]{sutton2019bitter}): methods that scale with compute and data beat cleverly hand-crafted ones. The transformer's **next-token** objective is *modality-agnostic* — it does not care whether the tokens are words, audio codes, or video patches — and attention gives it long-range reach at fixed depth. Same architecture, new vocabulary, more data. That is the whole recipe, and it is why one codebase keeps becoming the next breakthrough.
blocks.section: Why transformers won

blocks.quote: The two ways to generate
blocks.section: The two ways to generate

blocks.quote: Given a tokenizer that turns a signal into tokens, and a transformer engine, there are **two** fundamentally different ways to turn "a prompt" into "a song" or "a clip." They are both transformers at the core; they differ in *how the sequence is produced*. Knowing both is the key to reading every paper in this field.
blocks.section: The two ways to generate

blocks.quote: Family A: write it token by token (autoregressive)
blocks.section: Family A: write it token by token (autoregressive)

blocks.quote: This is the LLM way, applied to sound. The model predicts the **next token** given everything so far — exactly as GPT predicts the next word — and it just keeps going.
blocks.section: Family A: write it token by token (autoregressive)

blocks.quote: Next-token prediction, made musical
blocks.section: Next-token prediction, made musical

blocks.quote: At each step the network outputs a score for every code in the codec's vocabulary, a **softmax** turns that into a probability, and you **sample** one token. The sampling knob is where the *dice* come back into a story that began with dice:
blocks.section: Next-token prediction, made musical

blocks.quote: - **Temperature** divides the scores before the softmax. High temperature flattens the distribution (more surprises); low temperature sharpens it (more predictable).
blocks.section: Next-token prediction, made musical

blocks.quote: Change these knobs and you change how "on the nose" or "creative" a generated track sounds. It is the same sampling a chatbot uses to decide how to phrase its next sentence.
blocks.section: Next-token prediction, made musical

blocks.quote: Building a song in layers
blocks.section: Building a song in layers

blocks.quote: A whole song is too long to predict flatly, so the serious autoregressive machines build it **coarse-to-fine**, in layers of tokens at different rates:
blocks.section: Building a song in layers

blocks.quote: - **AudioLM** (Google, 2023) first autoregressively writes low-rate **semantic tokens** that carry long-range structure — *this is the verse, the harmony drifts here* — and then a second, non-autoregressive stage fills in the high-rate **acoustic tokens** (the actual codec codes) that a decoder turns back into sound (\cite[Borsos et al., 2023]{borsos2023audiolm}).
blocks.section: Building a song in layers

blocks.quote: - **MusicLM** (Google, 2023) does the same as a hierarchy: a **slow** transformer lays down melody, harmony and rhythm over long timescales, a **fast** transformer adds timbre and detail, and a vocoder renders audio — which is what lets it stay coherent for *minutes* (\cite[Agostinelli et al., 2023]{agostinelli2023musiqlm}).
blocks.section: Building a song in layers

blocks.quote: - **MusicGen** (Meta, 2023) is the lean, open, fast version: a single transformer over EnCodec's stacked codebooks, writing them token by token, steered by a text embedding (\cite[Copet et al., 2023]{copet2023musicgen}).
blocks.section: Building a song in layers

blocks.quote: MusicLM generates high-fidelity music from text descriptions such as "a calming violin melody backed by a distorted guitar riff", remaining consistent over several minutes.
blocks.section: Building a song in layers

blocks.quote: Family B: sculpt it out of noise (diffusion)
blocks.section: Family B: sculpt it out of noise (diffusion)

blocks.quote: The other family does not write tokens in order. It **denoises**. Start from pure static, and learn to push it — a little at a time — into a coherent signal, the way an image emerges from ink in water. (The full forward/reverse math is the **Diffusion Models** chapter \cite[Ho et al., 2020]{ho2020ddpm}; here is how it is applied to sound and video.)
blocks.section: Family B: sculpt it out of noise (diffusion)

blocks.quote: The latent space and the denoiser
blocks.section: The latent space and the denoiser

blocks.quote: You do not denoise 2.6 million waveform numbers or a million video pixels directly — it is too expensive. First a **variational autoencoder** (a VAE, \cite[Kingma & Welling, 2013]{kingma2014vae}) compresses the signal into a small **latent** space that keeps the important content and throws away the predictable detail. This is the same "space of coherent relations" from the vocabulary section, seen from the other end: the codec has folded the raw signal into the small set of coordinates the model actually reasons over. The diffusion process then runs in this compact space: a network is trained to predict *the noise that was added* at each of many steps, and at generation time you start from random latent noise and denoise it step by step until a clean, novel clip or track appears (\cite[Rombach et al., 2022]{rombach2022ldm}).
blocks.section: The latent space and the denoiser

blocks.quote: Classifier-free guidance: obeying the prompt
blocks.section: Classifier-free guidance: obeying the prompt

blocks.quote: The Diffusion Transformer: the unlock for video
blocks.section: The Diffusion Transformer: the unlock for video

blocks.quote: The original diffusion denoisers were **U-Nets** — convolutional image networks. In 2023, Peebles and Xie showed you can replace the U-Net with a **transformer that operates on patches** of the latent — a **Diffusion Transformer, or DiT** (\cite[Peebles & Xie, 2023]{peebles2023dit}). Two changes make it a big deal:
blocks.section: The Diffusion Transformer: the unlock for video

blocks.quote: - The latent is cut into a grid of **patches**, each patch becoming a **token**, and the transformer attends over all of them — so the denoiser is now structurally *the same family* as an LLM.
blocks.section: The Diffusion Transformer: the unlock for video

blocks.quote: - The timestep and the prompt are injected by **modulating the layer norms** (a trick called **adaLN**) rather than stitched in by hand, so the model always knows *how noisy* the input is and *what it was asked for*.
blocks.section: The Diffusion Transformer: the unlock for video

blocks.quote: This was the architectural unlock for video: once the denoiser was a transformer over patches, you could scale it with everything else — and that is exactly what Sora did.
blocks.section: The Diffusion Transformer: the unlock for video

blocks.quote: Video: the same engine, one dimension up
blocks.section: Video: the same engine, one dimension up

blocks.quote: Now the same story, one dimension up. A video is a stack of frames plus **time**, so the questions are the same three — *how do you represent it, how do you learn it, how do you tell it what to show?* — and the answers mirror the audio ones almost one for one.
blocks.section: Video: the same engine, one dimension up

blocks.quote: Analog moving pictures
blocks.section: Analog moving pictures

blocks.quote: The **cinema** began with the Lumière brothers' paid screenings in 1895: a strip of perforated film, a frame at a time, fast enough to look like motion. Home video came decades later as a **format war**: **Betamax** (Sony, 1975) against **VHS** (JVC, 1976), the latter winning; **LaserDisc** followed in 1978. The first consumer *digital* video format was the **DVD** (1996) — MPEG-2 video on an optical disc.
blocks.section: Analog moving pictures

blocks.quote: 35 mm film: motion is an illusion built from a chain of still frames, one at a time. The digital video that replaced it kept the "frames over time" idea and threw away the film. \cite[Photo: mannyisdead, CC BY 3.0]{film_strip_35mm_img}
blocks.section: Analog moving pictures

blocks.quote: VHS (1976), the analog home-video winner. A spinning helical head reads a magnetized tape — analog all the way through, until the DVD and the internet made video digital. \cite[Photo: LoMit, CC BY-SA 4.0]{vhs_cassette_img}
blocks.section: Analog moving pictures

blocks.quote: How a video codec really works
blocks.section: How a video codec really works

blocks.quote: Frames that borrow from their neighbours
blocks.section: Frames that borrow from their neighbours

blocks.quote: Video is a sequence of **frames**, and codecs classify them into three types \cite[How video is compressed]{video_compression}:
blocks.section: Frames that borrow from their neighbours

blocks.quote: - An **I-frame** (intra) is a complete picture, encoded on its own like a JPEG. It is the anchor, the keyframe every other frame leans on.
blocks.section: Frames that borrow from their neighbours

blocks.quote: - A **P-frame** (predictive) stores only the *difference* from the previous anchor, plus a **motion vector** saying how much each piece moved.
blocks.section: Frames that borrow from their neighbours

blocks.quote: - A **B-frame** (bi-directional) is predicted from the nearest anchor *in front of it and behind it*, giving the best compression — at the cost of being decoded out of order.
blocks.section: Frames that borrow from their neighbours

blocks.quote: Within a frame and across frames
blocks.section: Within a frame and across frames

blocks.quote: There are two compression moves, and together they are why a movie fits on a disc. **Within a frame (intra):** each 8×8 block of pixels is run through a **discrete cosine transform (DCT)**, turning it into frequencies; the high frequencies the eye barely sees are coarsely quantized (the lossy part), then entropy-coded \cite[The DCT]{dct}. **Across frames (inter):** **motion compensation** finds where each block moved since the last frame and stores the motion vector plus a small residual, instead of the whole block.
blocks.section: Within a frame and across frames

blocks.quote: The coding structure inside H.264/AVC for a single block: on the left, *intra* prediction (guess from neighbours in the same frame) and *inter* prediction (guess from a previous frame using a motion vector) both feed a DCT, quantization and entropy coding. This tiny diagram is the skeleton of almost every video you have ever streamed. \cite[Diagram: Alexandre Rebollal Lucas, public domain]{h264_coding_structure_img}
blocks.section: Within a frame and across frames

blocks.quote: The codec race is a long list of ever-better versions of exactly this: **MPEG-1** (1993, the first practical consumer digital video standard) → **H.264/AVC** (2003, the format of the streaming age) → **H.265/HEVC** (2013, ~half the bitrate) → **VP9** (2014) → **AV1** (2018, royalty-free, from the Alliance for Open Media) \cite[H.264/AVC]{h264} \cite[AV1]{av1}.
blocks.section: Within a frame and across frames

blocks.quote: The video tokenizer and the data
blocks.section: The video tokenizer and the data

blocks.quote: Just as audio got a neural codec, video got a **tokenizer**. In 2021, **VideoGPT** used a **VQ-VAE** to compress a video into **discrete spatio-temporal tokens** and then let a GPT-style model *write* the video token by token (\cite[Yan et al., 2021]{yan2021videogpt}) \cite[The VQ-VAE]{vq_vae}. **Video became a paragraph, too.**
blocks.section: The video tokenizer and the data

blocks.quote: The data problem is the same as for images and audio: you need millions of (clip, description) pairs. **WebVid-10M** (2021) scraped about ten million weakly-labelled video-text pairs from the web — the "LAION of video" (\cite[Bain et al., 2021]{bain2021webvid}). And the modern models go a step further and **re-caption** their clips: a powerful vision-language model rewrites a rich, accurate description for each clip, so the words actually match the pixels — the trick DALL·E 3 made famous.
blocks.section: The video tokenizer and the data

blocks.quote: Sora: a diffusion transformer that dreams a world
blocks.section: Sora: a diffusion transformer that dreams a world

blocks.quote: - A **3D video autoencoder** (a VAE) compresses the clip into a latent space, in space *and* time.
blocks.section: Sora: a diffusion transformer that dreams a world

blocks.quote: - The latent is cut into **spacetime patches** — small 3D cubes of pixels spanning a patch of an image *and* a few frames — and **those patches are the tokens**. (An image is just a video with one frame, so images and videos share one representation.)
blocks.section: Sora: a diffusion transformer that dreams a world

blocks.quote: - A **diffusion transformer** — the DiT of the previous section — denoises those 3D tokens, conditioned on the text prompt.
blocks.section: Sora: a diffusion transformer that dreams a world

blocks.quote: The remarkable part is not the pipeline but what *emerges at scale*. With no explicit 3D training signal, Sora begins to show **3D consistency** (objects move coherently as the camera orbits), **object permanence** (a character stays the same character across shots), and simple **physical interaction** (a painter's strokes persist; a bitten burger keeps its bite marks). OpenAI frames scaling video models as "a promising path towards building general-purpose simulators of the physical world."
blocks.section: Sora: a diffusion transformer that dreams a world

blocks.quote: Scaling video generation models is a promising path towards building general purpose simulators of the physical world.
blocks.section: Sora: a diffusion transformer that dreams a world

blocks.quote: That is the 2018 **World Models** dream — let a network learn a compressed model of an environment and act inside its own dream (\cite[Ha & Schmidhuber, 2018]{ha2018worldmodels}) — finally realized at internet scale. The caveats are real: it still gets physics wrong (glass that will not shatter like glass, food that will not run out), and long clips drift. But the direction is unmistakable. A machine is learning to *dream a plausible world from a seed.*
blocks.section: Sora: a diffusion transformer that dreams a world

blocks.quote: Bringing it all together
blocks.section: Bringing it all together

blocks.quote: How it works with the LLM, in one breath
blocks.section: How it works with the LLM, in one breath

blocks.quote: You have probably been wondering how any of this connects to a language model. Here is the whole answer:
blocks.section: How it works with the LLM, in one breath

blocks.quote: There are **two families**, and both are transformers with attention at their core.
blocks.section: How it works with the LLM, in one breath

blocks.quote: - **Autoregressive over tokens** (AudioLM, MusicGen, VideoGPT): the codec turns the signal into tokens, and the model predicts the *next token*, exactly like an LLM predicts the next word. Here the language model **is** the generator — it literally writes the audio or video, code by code.
blocks.section: How it works with the LLM, in one breath

blocks.quote: - **Diffusion over latents** (Stable Video Diffusion, Sora, AudioLDM): the signal lives in a continuous latent space, and a **diffusion transformer** learns to denoise it, while a transformer *encoder* reads the prompt and **classifier-free guidance** pushes the output toward it (\cite[Liu et al., 2023]{liu2023audioldm}).
blocks.section: How it works with the LLM, in one breath

blocks.quote: Either way the backbone is the same architecture that runs the chatbot you are reading this on. The **only** genuinely new ingredient per modality is the **tokenizer** — the learned codec that turns sound or frames into a vocabulary the Transformer can speak. Change the tokenizer, keep the engine.
blocks.section: How it works with the LLM, in one breath

blocks.quote: How much data, and how it lands in the tensors
blocks.section: How much data, and how it lands in the tensors

blocks.quote: The common thread: **the vocabulary is not letters, it is learned codes — and the corpus is internet-scale.** The model is not a hard drive of every song and clip ever made. It is a *compressed map of the space of possible sounds and scenes* — a landscape in which the meaningful regions form dense, well-connected clusters, joined by thin transition regions, with empty voids (nonsense) in between. Generating is not retrieving a stored item; it is *walking a path of coherence* through that landscape, one token at a time, steered by your prompt.
blocks.section: How much data, and how it lands in the tensors

blocks.quote: The flood, and the questions it raises
blocks.section: The flood, and the questions it raises

blocks.quote: The effects arrived fast. By late 2025, Deezer reported on the order of **50,000 AI-generated tracks uploaded a day — about a third of all uploads** — and began auto-tagging them and keeping them out of human-curated playlists; an AI-made country song reached the top of a Billboard chart. The law has not caught up: in the US the Copyright Office holds that **purely AI-generated works are not copyrightable** (no human author), and in the EU originality likewise requires a human's fingerprint. Meanwhile the labels fight back — **Universal Music Group and Sony Music sued Suno** for training on their catalog. So the field sits in a gap: a technology that can copy any voice or style, inside a legal system built on the assumption that a person made the thing.
blocks.section: The flood, and the questions it raises

blocks.quote: > In short. Same engine, two senses: *compress the signal into tokens, run a Transformer over them, steer it with a text embedding.* That one sentence is Suno, Udio, MusicGen, VideoGPT, Sora and the rest. Everything else is scale.
blocks.section: The flood, and the questions it raises

blocks.quote: The question, answered — differently
blocks.section: The question, answered — differently

blocks.quote: Zoom out and the story is one long arc with two turns. The first was philosophical: *remove the composer's hand* — Mozart's dice, Cage's stalks, Mälzel's self-playing organ, Xenakis' probabilities. The second is the one this chapter is about: *stop writing the rules, and let a big model infer them from the world* — until the machine can, from a sentence, dream a song or a world.
blocks.section: The question, answered — differently

blocks.quote: Music generation and video generation look like two different miracles to a first-time user. They are the same miracle seen from two angles: **a signal, compressed into tokens, then written by a transformer.** The dice are still there — a diffusion model "rolls the dice" in latent space at every denoising step, and a language model rolls them at every sampling step — but now the dice are guided by a prompt, and the table they roll on is a statistical model of reality.
blocks.section: The question, answered — differently

blocks.quote: More than two centuries after Mozart rolled the dice, the question "can a machine make something that feels made?" has a working, if contested, *yes*. The open questions are the human ones — who made it, who owns it, and what we do with a machine that can dream in audio and video.
